Question: A pure sample of the caraway form of carvone rotates plane-polarized light by +61°. Measured the same way (same concentration and tube), what rotation does the pure spearmint form, its enantiomer, give?
Feedback: Enantiomers rotate light by equal amounts in opposite directions, so the spearmint form gives −61°. 0° would be a 50:50 (racemic) mixture of the two, and +61° would mean the sample is the caraway form itself.

Question: The two mirror-image forms of thalidomide cannot be separated by distillation or by dissolving one in water. Why not?
Correct answer: Enantiomers have identical boiling points and identical solubility in water.
Distractors: Enantiomers have different boiling points, but both decompose when heated. | Diastereomers like these always form a racemic mixture. | The two forms are constitutional isomers with the same molecular mass.
Feedback: Mirror-image forms (enantiomers) have identical boiling points and solubility in ordinary (achiral) solvents, so distillation and simple dissolving cannot separate them. Separating enantiomers needs something chiral, such as a chiral column. The two forms are enantiomers, not diastereomers or constitutional isomers.

Question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3COCH2CH2OH?
Distractors: 1-hydroxy-3-butanone | 4-hydroxybutanal | 3-hydroxy-2-butanone
Feedback: Number from the end nearest the C=O: ketone on C2, –OH on C4: 4-hydroxy-2-butanone. 1-Hydroxy-3-butanone gives the ketone the higher number, and 3-hydroxy-2-butanone is a different compound, CH3COCH(OH)CH3.

Question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH2COOH, the compound responsible for the smell of rancid butter?
Distractors: propanoic acid | pentanoic acid | butanal
Feedback: Four carbons including the carboxyl carbon: butanoic acid (butyric acid). Forgetting to count the COOH carbon gives propanoic acid.

Question: Ethyl acetate, CH3COOCH2CH3, is a solvent in nail-polish remover. What is its IUPAC name?
Distractors: methyl propanoate | ethyl propanoate | propyl ethanoate
Feedback: The acid part is CH3CO– (ethanoate) and the alcohol part is ethyl: ethyl ethanoate. Methyl propanoate is an isomer, CH3CH2COOCH3.

Question: Propanoic acid reacts with methanol in the presence of an acid catalyst. What is the organic product?
Distractors: CH3COOCH2CH3 | CH3CH2OCH3 | CH3CH2CONHCH3
Feedback: CH3CH2COOH + HOCH3 → CH3CH2COOCH3 (methyl propanoate) + H2O. Ethyl ethanoate has the same formula but comes from acetic acid and ethanol.

Question: Which species are present in an aqueous solution of acetic acid (vinegar), besides water and CH3COOH molecules?
Distractors: CH+3 and COOH− | CH3COOH+2 and OH− | CH3CO+ and OH−
Feedback: The –COOH donates its H to water: CH3COOH + H2O ⇌ CH3COO− + H3O+. Only a small fraction ionizes, so most of the acid stays as molecules.

Question: What are the products of the neutralization of acetic acid with sodium hydroxide?
Distractors: ethyl alcohol and sodium oxide | sodium methanoate and water | ethanoic anhydride and NaH
Feedback: CH3COOH + NaOH → CH3COO−Na+ (sodium ethanoate, sodium acetate) + H2O. The carbon count of the acid does not change, so it is not a methanoate.

Question: Sodium benzoate is used as a food preservative instead of benzoic acid mainly because sodium benzoate
Correct answer: is ionic and more soluble in water
Distractors: is a stronger acid than benzoic acid | has a higher molar mass than benzoic acid | is nonpolar and dissolves in fats
Feedback: Carboxylate salts are ionic, so they dissolve far better in water than the acids, which have a large nonpolar ring. The same idea is used to make many drugs water-soluble.

Question: Propyl ethanoate (the odor of pears) is hydrolyzed in acid. What are the products?
Distractors: propanoic acid and ethanol | ethanol and 1-propanol | ethanoic acid and propane
Feedback: CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 + H2O → CH3COOH (ethanoic acid) + CH3CH2CH2OH (1-propanol). Swapping the parts gives propanoic acid and ethanol, the hydrolysis products of a different ester.

Question: Methyl butanoate is heated with aqueous NaOH (saponification). What are the products?
Distractors: butanoic acid and methanol | sodium methanoate and 1-butanol | butanoic acid and sodium methoxide
Feedback: Base hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt, sodium butanoate, and the alcohol, methanol. The free acid forms only in acid hydrolysis or after acidifying.

Question: These compounds all have molar mass 74 g mol⁻¹. Which has the highest boiling point?
Distractors: 1-butanol, CH3CH2CH2CH2OH | methyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH3 | diethyl ether, CH3CH2OCH2CH3
Feedback: Carboxylic acids form hydrogen-bonded dimers (two H bonds per pair), so propanoic acid (141 °C) boils above 1-butanol (118 °C). Esters and ethers have no O–H and boil much lower.

Question: Aspirin, acetylsalicylic acid, contains which two functional groups?
Correct answer: a carboxylic acid and an ester
Distractors: a phenol and an aldehyde | an alcohol and a ketone | an amide and an ether
Feedback: The original –COOH remains, and the phenol –OH becomes an acetyl ester, so aspirin has a carboxylic acid and an ester. Salicylic acid itself has the phenol group.

Question: Lactic acid, CH3CH(OH)COOH, is a carboxylic acid (a weak acid). In blood at pH 7.4, lactic acid exists mainly as
Distractors: neutral CH3CH(OH)COOH molecules | CH3CH(OH)COOH+2 ions | lactate esters
Feedback: Carboxylic acids are weak acids that give up their H+ at body pH (7.4), so lactic acid is present as the carboxylate ion, lactate. That is why we say “lactate” in physiology.

Question: This ester has a fruity smell: CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3. Choose its correct name.
Distractors: ethyl butanoate | propyl ethanoate | butyl propanoate
Feedback: The C=O side, CH3CH2CO–, has 3 carbons (propanoate); the alkyl on the O, –CH2CH2CH3, is propyl: propyl propanoate. "Ethyl butanoate" comes from splitting on the wrong side of the C=O carbon.

Question: Butanoic acid reacts with ethanol (H+, heat) to make ethyl butanoate, which smells like pineapple. Which is the ester?
Distractors: CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3 | CH3CH2CH2COCH2CH3 | CH3CH2CH2CH2OCH2CH3
Feedback: Esterification removes –OH from the acid and H from the alcohol (lost as H2O): CH3CH2CH2CO– + –OCH2CH3 = CH3CH2CH2COOCH2CH3. CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3 is an isomer (propyl propanoate) with the carbons split the wrong way.

Question: Isopentyl acetate, CH3COOCH2CH2CH(CH3)2, gives bananas their smell. Which acid and alcohol are used to make it?
Distractors: 3-methylbutanoic acid and methanol | acetic acid and 2-methyl-1-butanol | 3-methylbutanoic acid and ethanol
Feedback: CH3CO– is the acetate (acetic acid) part. The O–alkyl group –CH2CH2CH(CH3)2 came from HOCH2CH2CH(CH3)2, 3-methyl-1-butanol: acetic acid and 3-methyl-1-butanol.

Question: Isobutyl formate, HCOOCH2CH(CH3)2, adds a raspberry-like note to flavorings. If this ester undergoes acid-catalyzed hydrolysis, which products form?
Distractors: 2-methylpropanoic acid and methanol | sodium methanoate and 2-methyl-1-propanol | methanal and 2-methyl-1-propanol
Feedback: Breaking the C–O bond gives HCOOH (the C=O side) and HOCH2CH(CH3)2 (the O–alkyl side): methanoic acid and 2-methyl-1-propanol. Swapping the sides gives 2-methylpropanoic acid and methanol; a carboxylate salt only forms in base (NaOH), not in acid.

Question: Saponification of ethyl propanoate, CH3CH2COOCH2CH3, with NaOH yields which two products?
Distractors: propanoic acid and ethanol | sodium ethanoate and 1-propanol | propanoic acid and sodium ethoxide
Feedback: Saponification splits the ester at the C–O next to the C=O. The C=O side becomes the carboxylate salt CH3CH2COO−Na+ and the O–alkyl side becomes CH3CH2OH: sodium propanoate and ethanol. Propanoic acid itself would be the acid-hydrolysis product.

Question: Isocaproic acid, CH3CH(CH3)CH2CH2COOH, has an unpleasant cheesy odor. Which IUPAC name is correct for this acid?
Distractors: 2-methylpentanoic acid | 4-methylhexanoic acid | 4-methylpentanal
Feedback: The carboxyl carbon is C1; the chain has 5 carbons and the CH3 is on C4: 4-methylpentanoic acid. Counting the branch carbon into the chain (hexanoic) or numbering from the other end (2-methyl) are the usual slips; "-al" would mean an aldehyde.

Question: After it is swallowed, aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) is hydrolyzed at its ester group by enzymes in the body. Which two products form?
Distractors: salicylic acid and ethanol | benzoic acid and acetic acid | salicylic acid and methanol
Feedback: Aspirin's ester is Ar–O–CO–CH3. Hydrolysis breaks that C–O bond: the C=O side becomes acetic acid and the O side becomes the phenol –OH of salicylic acid: salicylic acid and acetic acid. Methanol would come from methyl salicylate, a different ester.

Question: An ester is written as CH3–O–CO–CH2CH3. Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of it produces which pair?
Distractors: acetic acid and ethanol | methanoic acid and 1-propanol | sodium propanoate and methanol
Feedback: The C=O carbon is bonded to –CH2CH3, so the acid part is CH3CH2COOH (3 C); the –OCH3 becomes methanol. This is methyl propanoate, so the products are propanoic acid and methanol. Acetic acid and ethanol would come from its isomer ethyl ethanoate.

Question: An ester is hydrolyzed once with aqueous acid and once with aqueous NaOH. How do the organic products differ?
Correct answer: Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid; base hydrolysis gives its carboxylate salt. The alcohol released is the same.
Distractors: Acid hydrolysis gives the carboxylate salt; base hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid. The alcohol released is the same. | Acid hydrolysis gives an alcohol; base hydrolysis gives an aldehyde instead. | The products are identical; only the reaction rate differs.
Feedback: Both reactions cut the ester at the C–O single bond, releasing the alcohol. In acid the carbonyl piece is the free carboxylic acid; in NaOH the acid is neutralized to the sodium carboxylate salt (saponification). No aldehyde forms in either case, and the products are not identical because the salt is ionic.

Question: Ant stings contain HCOOH. What is its IUPAC name?
Distractors: methanol | methanal | ethanoic acid
Feedback: One carbon with a carboxyl group: methanoic acid (common name formic acid). Methanol is an alcohol and methanal an aldehyde.

Question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2COOH?
Distractors: propanol | propanal | butanoic acid
Feedback: Three carbons, the COOH carbon is C1: propanoic acid.

Question: Which carboxylic acid is the most soluble in water?
Distractors: hexanoic acid (6 C) | octanoic acid (8 C) | decanoic acid (10 C)
Feedback: Small acids (up to about 4 carbons) mix with water; each extra CH2 adds nonpolar surface, so ethanoic acid is the most soluble.

Question: Acetic acid (60 g mol⁻¹) boils at 118 °C, higher than 1-propanol (60 g mol⁻¹, 97 °C). Why?
Correct answer: two acetic acid molecules hydrogen bond to each other twice, forming dimers
Distractors: acetic acid is an ionic compound | 1-propanol cannot hydrogen bond | acetic acid has more dispersion forces because it has more carbons
Feedback: Carboxylic acids pair up into hydrogen-bonded dimers (two H bonds per pair), so they boil higher than alcohols of similar molar mass.

Question: Esters boil at much lower temperatures than carboxylic acids of similar molar mass because esters
Correct answer: have no O–H group, so they cannot hydrogen bond to one another
Distractors: are ionic | have no polar bonds | are always smaller molecules
Feedback: An ester has C=O and C–O–C but no O–H, so ester molecules attract each other only by dipole–dipole and dispersion forces.

Question: Which compound is the strongest acid?
Distractors: phenol, C6H5OH | ethanol, CH3CH2OH | water
Feedback: Acid strength: carboxylic acid > phenol > water ≈ alcohol. The carboxylate ion is stabilized because its negative charge is shared by two oxygens.

Question: What is the name of CH3COO−Na+?
Distractors: sodium acetic acid | acetyl sodium | methyl sodium carbonate
Feedback: The metal is named first, and the acid ending -ic acid becomes -ate: sodium acetate (IUPAC: sodium ethanoate).

Question: 1-Butanol is heated with excess K2Cr2O7. Which carboxylic acid forms?
Distractors: propanoic acid | butanal only | 2-butanone
Feedback: A primary alcohol with excess oxidizing agent goes alcohol → aldehyde → butanoic acid, keeping all four carbons.

Question: Glucose 6-phosphate, the first product of glycolysis, is an ester of phosphoric acid and
Distractors: a carboxylic acid | an amine | another phosphoric acid
Feedback: Phosphoric acid condenses with the –OH on carbon 6 of glucose, losing water, to make a phosphate ester.

Question: An unknown white solid dissolves in 5% NaHCO3(aq) with bubbles of CO2. Which compound could it be?
Distractors: phenol, C6H5OH | cyclohexanol, C6H11OH | naphthalene, C10H8
Feedback: Carboxylic acids are the only common organic acids strong enough to react with NaHCO3: RCOOH + NaHCO3 → RCOO−Na+ + H2O + CO2. The bubbles point to benzoic acid, which dissolves as sodium benzoate.

Question: Cream of tartar, a by-product of making wine from Valley grapes, is potassium hydrogen tartrate: tartaric acid with one –COOH still present. Baking powder mixes it with baking soda (NaHCO3). When water is added, CO2 bubbles form. Which part of the cream of tartar causes this?
Correct answer: its remaining –COOH group, which is acidic enough to react with NaHCO3
Distractors: its two alcohol –OH groups, which react with NaHCO3 | the K+ ion, which reacts with water to give CO2 | its C–H bonds, which are oxidized by NaHCO3
Feedback: Only a carboxylic acid group reacts with NaHCO3 to release CO2: –COOH + HCO3− → –COO− + H2O + CO2. The remaining –COOH group of the hydrogen tartrate supplies the H+, and the gas makes the batter rise.

Question: Propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH, has the same molecular formula as which ester?
Distractors: CH3CH2COOCH3 | CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 | HCOOCH3
Feedback: Methyl ethanoate CH3COOCH3 is C3H6O2, a functional-group isomer of propanoic acid: CH3COOCH3. Methyl propanoate has 4 carbons because the methyl on O counts too.

Question: What is the IUPAC name of HOCH2CH2CH2COOH?
Distractors: 1-hydroxybutanoic acid | 4-hydroxybutanal | 3-hydroxypropanoic acid
Feedback: The –COOH carbon is C1 of a 4-carbon chain, and the –OH is on C4 as a hydroxy prefix: 4-hydroxybutanoic acid. 3-Hydroxypropanoic acid forgets that the COOH carbon is part of the chain.

Question: What is the IUPAC name of CH3CH2CH(CH3)COOH?
Distractors: 3-methylbutanoic acid | 2-methylpentanoic acid | 1-methylpropanoic acid
Feedback: The longest chain that includes the COOH carbon has four carbons (butanoic acid). The COOH carbon is carbon 1, so the CH3 branch is on carbon 2: 2-methylbutanoic acid.

Question: The ketone body 3-hydroxybutanoic acid (β-hydroxybutyric acid) builds up in the blood in uncontrolled diabetes. Which condensed formula is this compound?
Distractors: CH3CH2CH(OH)COOH | HOCH2CH2CH2COOH | CH3CH(OH)CH2CH2COOH
Feedback: Butanoic acid has four carbons, with the COOH carbon as carbon 1. The OH belongs on carbon 3, two carbons away from the COOH carbon: CH3CH(OH)CH2COOH.

Question: Formic acid and acetic acid are the common names of the two smallest carboxylic acids. What are their condensed formulas, in that order?
Distractors: CH3COOH and CH3CH2COOH | CH3COOH and HCOOH | HCOOH and CH3CH2COOH
Feedback: Formic acid (methanoic acid) has one carbon, the COOH carbon itself: HCOOH. Acetic acid (ethanoic acid) has two: HCOOH and CH3COOH.

Question: The name 3-methylpentanoic acid gives a number for the methyl group but none for the carboxyl group. Why is no number needed?
Correct answer: The carboxyl carbon is always at the end of the parent chain and is always carbon 1.
Distractors: The carboxyl carbon is a substituent and is not counted as part of the parent chain. | The carboxyl group can be on any carbon, so its position is left out of the name. | Positions in carboxylic acids are given only with Greek letters, never with numbers.
Feedback: A COOH carbon has only one bond left for the chain, so it must be at the end. Numbering starts there, so the carboxyl carbon is always carbon 1 and writing the 1 would add nothing.

Question: Which compound is a carboxylic acid?
Distractors: CH3CH2CH2OH | CH3COCH3 | HOCH2COCH3
Feedback: A carboxylic acid has a C=O and an OH on the same carbon, written –COOH. Only CH3CH2COOH has that group.

Question: Which condensed formula is methyl propanoate?
Distractors: CH3COOCH2CH2CH3 | CH3CH2CH2COOCH3 | CH3CH2COOCH2CH3
Feedback: Propanoate is the three-carbon acid part, CH3CH2CO–, counting the C=O carbon. Methyl is the CH3 on the oxygen. Together: CH3CH2COOCH3.

Question: Pentyl ethanoate (pentyl acetate), CH3COOCH2CH2CH2CH2CH3, has a pear-like odor. Which acid and which alcohol do the two parts of this ester come from?
Distractors: pentanoic acid and ethanol | ethanoic acid and pentanoic acid | 1-pentanol and ethanol
Feedback: The -ate word comes from the acid: ethanoate from ethanoic acid (the CH3CO– part). The -yl word is the group on the oxygen, which comes from the alcohol: pentyl from 1-pentanol.

Question: What is the IUPAC name of HCOOCH2CH3?
Distractors: methyl ethanoate | ethyl ethanoate | propanoic acid
Feedback: The acid part is HCO–, one carbon, so it is methanoate. The group on the single-bonded oxygen is CH2CH3, ethyl. The name is ethyl methanoate (ethyl formate).

Question: Which compound is an ester?
Distractors: CH3CH2CH2CH2COOH | CH3CH2OCH2CH2CH3 | CH3COCH2OCH2CH3
Feedback: In CH3CH2COOCH2CH3 the C=O carbon is bonded to a second oxygen, and that oxygen is bonded to an ethyl group. That –COO–C pattern is an ester (ethyl propanoate).

Question: In propyl ethanoate, CH3COOCH2CH2CH3, how many carbon atoms belong to the acid part and how many to the alcohol part?
Correct answer: 2 in the acid part, 3 in the alcohol part
Distractors: 3 in the acid part, 2 in the alcohol part | 1 in the acid part, 4 in the alcohol part | 1 in the acid part and 3 in the alcohol part; the C=O carbon belongs to neither
Feedback: The acid part is CH3CO–, which has 2 carbons counting the C=O carbon (ethanoate). The alcohol part is the propyl group on the oxygen, with 3 carbons.

Question: Dimethylamine, (CH3)2NH, is classified as a
Distractors: primary (1°) amine | tertiary (3°) amine | secondary amide
Feedback: Nitrogen carries two methyl groups and one H, so it is a 2° amine. It has no C=O, so it is not an amide.

Question: sec-Butylamine, CH3CH2CH(NH2)CH3, is classified as a
Distractors: secondary (2°) amine | tertiary (3°) amine | quaternary ammonium ion
Feedback: The N is bonded to only one carbon (and two H), so it is a 1° amine. The “sec” describes the alkyl group's carbon, not the amine class; that is the trap behind the 2° answer.

Question: What is the common name of CH3CH2CH2NH2?
Distractors: isopropylamine | propanamide | dipropylamine
Feedback: The straight three-carbon group on N is propyl: propylamine. Isopropylamine is (CH3)2CHNH2; propanamide would have a C=O.

Question: Which condensed formula is tert-butylamine?
Distractors: CH3CH2CH(NH2)CH3 | CH3CH2CH2CH2NH2 | (CH3)2CHCH2NH2
Feedback: tert-Butyl is (CH3)3C–, so tert-butylamine is (CH3)3CNH2. The others are sec-butylamine, butylamine and isobutylamine.

Question: Methylamine is a weak base. Which ions form when it dissolves in water?
Distractors: CH3NH− and H3O+ | CH+3 and NH−2 | CH3NH+3 and H3O+
Feedback: CH3NH2 + H2O ⇌ CH3NH+3 + OH−. The amine is the proton acceptor, so hydroxide ions form and the solution is basic.

Question: Many amine drugs, such as diphenhydramine, are sold as hydrochloride salts. Why?
Correct answer: The ionic salt is more soluble in water and body fluids.
Distractors: The salt is a stronger base than the free amine. | The salt is more volatile, so it is absorbed faster. | HCl converts the amine into a more stable amide.
Feedback: Amine + HCl → ammonium chloride salt. The ionic salt dissolves well in water and is a stable, odorless solid. It is not an amide, and salts are less volatile, not more.

Question: Which isomer of C3H9N has the lowest boiling point?
Distractors: propylamine, CH3CH2CH2NH2 | ethylmethylamine, CH3CH2NHCH3 | isopropylamine, (CH3)2CHNH2
Feedback: A 3° amine has no H on nitrogen, so it cannot H-bond to itself; trimethylamine boils at only ~3 °C. The 1° and 2° isomers have N–H bonds, so they hydrogen bond and boil higher (about 32–48 °C).

Question: Propanoic acid is heated with methylamine. What is the organic product of this amidation?
Distractors: N-propylmethanamide | methyl propanoate | propylmethylamine
Feedback: CH3CH2COOH + H2NCH3 → CH3CH2CONHCH3 + H2O: N-methylpropanamide. Methyl propanoate would come from methanol, not methylamine.

Question: N-Ethylethanamide, CH3CONHCH2CH3, is heated with aqueous NaOH. What are the products?
Distractors: ethanoic acid and ethylammonium ion | ethanol and ethanamide | sodium ethanoate and ammonia
Feedback: Hydrolysis breaks the C–N bond; in NaOH the acid becomes sodium ethanoate and the N part is released as ethylamine. Acid hydrolysis would instead give the free acid and the ammonium salt; ammonia would come only from an unsubstituted amide.

Question: Nicotine, caffeine and morphine are physiologically active nitrogen-containing compounds from plants. They are called
Distractors: amino acids | steroids | terpenes
Feedback: Plant-derived, biologically active amines are alkaloids. Many medicines (codeine, quinine, atropine) come from this group.

Question: Nylon 6,6, used in sutures, is a polyamide made from hexanedioic acid and 1,6-hexanediamine. What linkage joins the monomers?
Distractors: ester (–COO–) | ether (–O–) | glycosidic (C–O–C between sugars)
Feedback: Each –COOH reacts with an –NH2 to form an amide bond, releasing water; that is why nylon is a polyamide. Polyesters such as PET use ester linkages.

Question: Choline, (CH3)3N+CH2CH2OH, is needed to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine. How is its nitrogen classified?
Distractors: tertiary (3°) amine | secondary (2°) amine | primary (1°) amine
Feedback: Nitrogen is bonded to four carbons (three CH3 and one CH2) and carries a + charge: quaternary ammonium ion. A tertiary amine has only three carbons on a neutral N.

Question: Acetaminophen is an amide, HO–C6H4–NH–C(=O)–CH3. Which carboxylic acid and amine could form it by condensation?
Distractors: 4-hydroxybenzoic acid and methylamine | acetic acid and phenol | formic acid and 4-aminophenol
Feedback: The C(=O)CH3 piece is from acetic acid, and the HO–C6H4–NH– piece is from the amine 4-aminophenol: acetic acid and 4-aminophenol. 4-Hydroxybenzoic acid + methylamine would put the C=O on the ring side, a different compound.

Question: How is tetramethylammonium chloride, (CH3)4N+ Cl−, classified?
Distractors: tertiary ammonium salt | tertiary amine | primary amine salt
Feedback: Nitrogen has four C–N bonds, no N–H and a + charge, so this is a quaternary ammonium salt. A tertiary amine has three carbon groups and a neutral N; its salt, R3NH+, still has an N–H.

Question: Methamphetamine is C6H5CH2CH(CH3)NHCH3. Its amine group is classified as
Distractors: primary (1°) | tertiary (3°) | quaternary
Feedback: The N is bonded to two carbons (the CH and the CH3) and one H: secondary (2°). Calling it 1° comes from using the alcohol rule (looking at the carbon) instead of counting carbons on N.

Question: How would you name CH3NHCH2CH3, a secondary amine, using common (alkyl + amine) naming?
Distractors: propylamine | diethylamine | N-methylethanamide
Feedback: The N carries one ethyl and one methyl group: ethylmethylamine, a 2° amine. Propylamine has all three carbons in one chain, and an "-amide" would need a C=O on the N.

Question: Dimethylamine, (CH3)2NH, and acetic acid are heated together and water is driven off. Which amide forms?
Distractors: CH3CONHCH3 | CH3CH2N(CH3)2 | HCON(CH3)2
Feedback: The acid's –OH and the N–H combine as H2O and the new C–N bond joins CH3CO– to –N(CH3)2: CH3CON(CH3)2, N,N-dimethylethanamide. CH3CONHCH3 loses one of the amine's methyl groups.

Question: When ethylamine, CH3CH2NH2, is mixed with hydrochloric acid, which substance is formed?
Distractors: CH3CH2Cl + NH3 | CH3CH2NHCl + H2 | CH3CH2NH− + H3O+
Feedback: The lone pair on N accepts H+ from HCl, giving the salt CH3CH2NH+3 Cl− (ethylammonium chloride). Nothing is substituted; it is a simple acid–base (neutralization) reaction.

Question: Hot aqueous HCl hydrolyzes propanamide, CH3CH2CONH2. Which products result?
Distractors: sodium propanoate and NH3 | 1-propanol and NH4Cl | propanamine and H2O
Feedback: Water splits the C–N bond: the C=O side becomes CH3CH2COOH and the N side is NH3, which picks up H+ in acid: propanoic acid and NH4Cl. A sodium salt plus NH3 is what forms in NaOH instead.

Question: Name the amide CH3CH2CH2CH2CONHCH3 using IUPAC rules.
Distractors: N-methylhexanamide | N-pentylmethanamide | N-methylpentanamine
Feedback: The C=O chain, CH3CH2CH2CH2CO–, has 5 carbons (pentanamide) and the CH3 on N is named N-methyl: N-methylpentanamide. Counting the N–CH3 into the chain gives the wrong "hexanamide"; "-amine" ignores the C=O.

Question: Which compound will NOT form an amide when heated with acetic acid?
Distractors: (CH3)2NH | CH3NH2 | NH3
Feedback: Forming the amide removes –OH from the acid and an H from N. (CH3)3N, a 3° amine, has no N–H, so it can only form a salt with the acid, not an amide. NH3, 1° and 2° amines all have N–H.

Question: Fish smells "fishy" partly because of volatile amines such as trimethylamine. Squeezing lemon juice on fish reduces the odor mainly because
Correct answer: the acid converts the amines into nonvolatile ammonium salts
Distractors: the acid converts the amines into amides | the acid oxidizes the amines to carboxylic acids | the acid converts the amines into esters
Feedback: Citric acid donates H+ to the amine N, forming an ammonium salt. The ionic salt is water-soluble and not volatile, so it does not reach your nose. Amides would require heating, and a 3° amine cannot form one.

Question: Which statement best describes a neurotransmitter?
Correct answer: a chemical messenger released by a nerve cell that crosses a synapse and binds to receptors on the next cell
Distractors: a hormone carried by the blood to organs far from where it is made | an enzyme that breaks down nerve signals in the brain | the electrical signal that travels along a nerve fiber
Feedback: A neurotransmitter is a chemical messenger released by a nerve cell. It crosses the synapse, binds to receptors on the next cell, and is then removed or broken down. Many neurotransmitters are amines, such as dopamine and serotonin.

Question: Dopamine, norepinephrine, serotonin and histamine are all neurotransmitters. Which functional group do all four contain, which is protonated (–NH3+) at body pH?
Distractors: an amide | a carboxylic acid | an ester
Feedback: All four contain an amine group. Like other amines, it is a weak base and is mostly protonated in body fluids, so these neurotransmitters carry a positive charge.

Question: SSRI antidepressants such as fluoxetine (Prozac) block the reuptake of serotonin, the step in which the sending nerve cell takes serotonin back in from the synapse. What is the effect?
Correct answer: Serotonin stays in the synapse longer, so its signal to the next cell lasts longer
Distractors: The body stops making serotonin | Serotonin is broken down faster in the synapse | Serotonin can no longer bind to its receptors
Feedback: Reuptake normally clears serotonin from the synapse and ends its signal. Blocking it means serotonin stays in the synapse longer and keeps acting on the receptors of the next cell.

Question: Ammonia (NH3) from dairies and fertilizer reacts in Valley air with nitric acid (HNO3) from vehicle exhaust, forming tiny particles of ammonium nitrate, NH4NO3. In this reaction, ammonia acts as
Correct answer: a base that accepts H+ to form the ammonium ion
Distractors: an acid that donates H+ | an oxidizing agent | a catalyst that is not changed
Feedback: Like an amine, ammonia uses its nitrogen lone pair to accept H+ from the acid, forming NH4+. The product, ammonium nitrate, is an ammonium salt, just like the salt formed when an amine reacts with HCl.

Question: In which reaction does water act as an acid?
Distractors: CH3COOH + H2O → CH3COO− + H3O+ | HCl + H2O → Cl− + H3O+ | HCOOH + H2O → HCOO− + H3O+
Feedback: With the amine (a base), water donates H+ and becomes OH−: CH3NH2 + H2O. With acids (HCl, carboxylic acids) water accepts H+ to form H3O+, so there it is a base.

Question: Fructose, C6H12O6, has its carbonyl group on carbon 2. Fructose is classified as a(n)
Distractors: aldohexose | ketopentose | aldopentose
Feedback: A C=O on C2 (not the end) makes a ketone, and six carbons make a hexose: ketohexose. Glucose and galactose are aldohexoses.

Question: In the Haworth projection of α-D-glucose, the –OH group on carbon 1 is
Correct answer: below the ring, opposite the CH2OH group
Distractors: above the ring, on the same side as the CH2OH group | in the plane of the ring | replaced by the ring oxygen
Feedback: In a D-sugar the CH2OH points up; in the α anomer the C1 –OH points down, opposite it. The β anomer has the C1 –OH up.

Question: For an aldohexose drawn as a Fischer projection, which carbon's –OH position determines whether the sugar is D or L?
Distractors: carbon 1 | carbon 2 | carbon 6
Feedback: C5 is the chiral carbon farthest from the C=O, so carbon 5 decides: an –OH on the right makes it D. C1 and C6 are not chiral at all.

Question: When glucose forms its six-membered ring, the –OH on carbon 5 adds to the carbonyl group on carbon 1. The ring is a cyclic
Distractors: acetal | ester | hemiketal
Feedback: One alcohol (the C5 –OH) adding to an aldehyde (C1) forms a hemiacetal. A glycosidic bond to a second sugar turns it into an acetal. A hemiketal would form from a ketone sugar such as fructose.

Question: In the five-membered ring form of fructose, the anomeric carbon (the one whose –OH can be α or β) is carbon
Feedback: Fructose's C=O is on C2, so after cyclization C2 is the anomeric carbon. C1 is the anomeric carbon only in aldoses such as glucose.

Question: In poorly controlled diabetes, excess glucose in the lens of the eye is converted to sorbitol, which contributes to cataracts. Sorbitol is
Correct answer: a sugar alcohol formed by reducing the aldehyde of glucose
Distractors: a carboxylic acid formed by oxidizing the aldehyde of glucose | a disaccharide formed by joining two glucose molecules | a ketose formed by moving the carbonyl of glucose to C2
Feedback: Reduction of the aldehyde (–CHO) on C1 of glucose gives a primary alcohol (–CH2OH), so sorbitol (glucitol) is a sugar alcohol. Oxidizing the aldehyde would give gluconic acid, a carboxylic acid. Sorbitol is also used as a sugar-free sweetener.

Question: Ribulose, an intermediate in photosynthesis and the pentose phosphate pathway, has the open-chain structure CH2OH–CO–CHOH–CHOH–CH2OH. How is ribulose classified?
Distractors: aldopentose | ketohexose | aldotetrose
Feedback: Ribulose has 5 carbons (pentose) and its C=O is on carbon 2, inside the chain, so it is a ketone: ketopentose. An aldopentose (like ribose) has the C=O on carbon 1 as –CHO.

Question: D-Glucose cyclizes to form β-D-glucopyranose, a six-membered ring. How many chiral carbons does β-D-glucopyranose have?
Feedback: Open-chain glucose has 4 chiral carbons (C2–C5). On ring closure, C1 becomes a hemiacetal carbon bonded to –OH, –O– (ring), –H and C2: four different groups, so it is a new chiral center. Total: 5. C6 (–CH2OH) is never chiral.

Question: Maltose is two glucose units joined by an α(1→4) linkage. Which statement correctly describes carbon 1 of each glucose unit in maltose?
Correct answer: The linked C1 is an acetal; the other C1 is a hemiacetal
Distractors: Both C1 carbons are acetals, so maltose is not reducing | Both C1 carbons are hemiacetals, held by an ester bond | The linked C1 is a hemiacetal; the other C1 is an acetal
Feedback: C1 of the first glucose bears the ring O and the glycosidic O (two –OR groups): an acetal. C1 of the second glucose still has a free –OH and the ring O: a hemiacetal, which can open to an aldehyde, so maltose is a reducing sugar.

Question: How is the enantiomer of D-glucose drawn in a Fischer projection?
Correct answer: L-glucose: the –OH on all chiral carbons is moved to the opposite side
Distractors: L-glucose: only the –OH on carbon 5 is moved to the opposite side | β-D-glucose: only the –OH on carbon 1 is moved to the opposite side | D-galactose: only the –OH on carbon 4 is moved to the opposite side
Feedback: An enantiomer is the mirror image, so all four chiral centers (C2–C5) are reversed, giving L-glucose. Flipping only C5 gives a different sugar (a diastereomer, not glucose); flipping only C4 gives galactose, an epimer.

Question: α-D-Glucose and β-D-glucose are called anomers because they differ only in
Correct answer: the position of the –OH on the hemiacetal carbon, C1
Distractors: the position of the –OH on carbon 5, which sets D or L | the position of the –OH on carbon 4 of the ring | the size of the ring, five-membered versus six-membered
Feedback: Ring closure makes C1 (the anomeric carbon) a new chiral center, so the –OH there can be down (α) or up (β): anomers differ only at C1. Differing only at C4 makes epimers such as glucose and galactose.

Question: An aldohexose is drawn as a Fischer projection. Reading from C2 down to C5, its –OH groups point right, left, left, right. Which sugar is it?
Distractors: L-galactose | D-mannose | D-glucose
Feedback: D-glucose is right, left, right, right. This sugar differs only at C4, which makes it galactose, and the –OH on C5 points right, so it is D-galactose. L-galactose would have every –OH reversed, not just one.

Question: In the Fischer projection of D-mannose, the –OH groups on C2, C3, C4 and C5 point left, left, right, right. How are these –OH groups drawn in L-mannose?
Distractors: left, left, right, left | right, right, left, right | left, left, right, right
Feedback: Enantiomers are mirror images, so every chiral –OH switches sides: left, left, right, right → right, right, left, left. Flipping only C5 (left, left, right, left) gives a different sugar (a diastereomer), not the enantiomer.

Question: D-Ribose is an aldopentose. How many chiral carbons does its open-chain form have, and how many stereoisomers (2n) are possible for an aldopentose?
Distractors: 4 chiral carbons; 16 stereoisomers | 3 chiral carbons; 6 stereoisomers | 5 chiral carbons; 32 stereoisomers
Feedback: C1 (–CHO) and C5 (–CH2OH) are not chiral, so C2, C3 and C4 are: n = 3, and 23 = 8 stereoisomers (3 chiral carbons). Counting all 5 carbons as chiral is the common mistake.

Question: Dihydroxyacetone, HOCH2–CO–CH2OH, is the active ingredient in sunless tanning lotions. How is it classified?
Distractors: aldotriose | ketotetrose | ketopentose
Feedback: It has 3 carbons (triose), and the C=O is on the middle carbon, so it is a ketone: a ketotriose. Its isomer glyceraldehyde, with –CHO at C1, is the aldotriose.

Question: Compare open-chain D-glucose with D-mannose: same formula, but the C2 –OH points left in mannose and right in glucose, with C3–C5 identical. What is the relationship?
Distractors: They are enantiomers. | They are anomers. | They are structural isomers.
Feedback: Stereoisomers that differ at only one chiral carbon are epimers. Enantiomers differ at every chiral carbon; anomers differ only at the anomeric carbon of a ring (C1), not at C2 of the open chain.

Question: A Haworth projection of a D-hexopyranose shows the –OH on C1 pointing up, the –OH on C2 pointing down, the –OH on C3 pointing up and the –OH on C4 pointing up. Which sugar is it?
Distractors: α-D-galactose | β-D-glucose | α-D-glucose
Feedback: The C1 –OH is up, so it is β. Glucose has its C4 –OH down; here C4 is up, so it is galactose (the C4 epimer): β-D-galactose. Calling it glucose misses the C4 difference.

Question: Isomaltose, a product of starch digestion at the branch points, joins two glucose units: the α anomeric carbon of one unit links via –O– to C6 of the other. Which label describes this bond?
Feedback: The first glucose uses its α anomeric carbon (C1), and it joins C6 of the next unit: α(1→6), the same link found at the branch points of amylopectin and glycogen.

Question: In sucrose, C1 of glucose and C2 of fructose are both used in the glycosidic bond. Which functional groups are present at these two anomeric carbons?
Correct answer: an acetal at glucose C1 and a ketal at fructose C2
Distractors: a hemiacetal at glucose C1 and a hemiketal at fructose C2 | a hemiacetal at glucose C1 and a ketal at fructose C2 | a ketal at glucose C1 and an acetal at fructose C2
Feedback: Both anomeric carbons carry two –O–R groups and no free –OH, so neither is 'hemi'. Glucose C1 (from an aldehyde) is an acetal, fructose C2 (from a ketone) is a ketal. With no hemiacetal left, sucrose is not a reducing sugar.

Question: Glucose gives a positive Benedict's test (a reducing sugar) but sucrose does not. Which structural feature makes glucose a reducing sugar?
Correct answer: Its ring can open to a free aldehyde (hemiacetal carbon not locked in a glycosidic bond)
Distractors: It has five –OH groups that are easily oxidized | Its ring oxygen can accept electrons from Cu2+ | It contains an acetal carbon that is oxidized to a carboxylic acid
Feedback: In solution the cyclic hemiacetal of glucose opens to the free aldehyde, which Cu2+ oxidizes to a carboxylate (red Cu2O forms), so a free hemiacetal/aldehyde makes a sugar reducing. In sucrose both anomeric carbons are tied up as an acetal and a ketal, so no aldehyde can form. The alcohol –OH groups are not oxidized by Benedict's reagent.

Question: In its five-membered ring form, fructose has an –OH group and the ring oxygen both attached to carbon 2, which also bears two carbon groups. What functional group is at C2?
Distractors: Hemiacetal | Ketal | Ketone
Feedback: When the C5 –OH adds to the C2 ketone, the carbon ends up with –OH, –OR (the ring O) and two carbon substituents: a hemiketal. A hemiacetal would have an H on that carbon (from an aldose such as glucose); a ketal needs two –OR groups and forms only when the sugar makes a glycosidic bond.

Question: A disaccharide is hydrolyzed to two D-glucose molecules. Benedict's test on the intact disaccharide is positive, and the enzyme that digests it in humans is maltase, not lactase or cellulase. Which linkage joins the two rings?
Correct answer: α(1→4), with one free hemiacetal carbon
Distractors: β(1→4), with one free hemiacetal carbon | α,β(1→2), with no free hemiacetal carbon | α(1→6), with the two anomeric carbons used
Feedback: Maltose is the glucose–glucose disaccharide hydrolyzed by maltase, joined α(1→4); its second ring keeps a free hemiacetal at C1, which opens to an aldehyde and reduces Cu2+. A β(1→4) glucose pair is cellobiose (from cellulose, not digestible); α,β(1→2) is sucrose, which is non-reducing because both anomeric carbons are used.

Question: Warm nitric acid, a strong oxidizing agent, oxidizes both C1 (the aldehyde) and C6 (the –CH2OH) of glucose to –COOH. What is the product?
Distractors: gluconic acid, an aldonic acid | glucuronic acid, a uronic acid | sorbitol, a sugar alcohol
Feedback: When both ends become –COOH, the product is a dicarboxylic acid called an aldaric acid: glucaric acid. Oxidizing only C1 gives gluconic acid (aldonic), and oxidizing only C6 gives glucuronic acid (uronic).

Question: When pure α-D-glucose is dissolved in water, the solution soon contains α-D-glucose, β-D-glucose and a little open-chain glucose. This process is called
Distractors: hydrolysis | fermentation | isomerization to fructose
Feedback: Interconversion of the α and β anomers through the open-chain form is mutarotation; no bonds to other molecules are broken, so it is not hydrolysis.

Question: D-Galactose differs from D-glucose only in the position of the –OH group on carbon
Feedback: Galactose is the C-4 epimer of glucose. Changing C2 gives mannose; changing C5 would change D to L.

Question: Which sugar is NOT a reducing sugar?
Distractors: maltose | lactose | glucose
Feedback: In sucrose, both anomeric carbons are tied up in the glycosidic bond, so it cannot open and gives a negative Benedict's test. Maltose, lactose and glucose are reducing.

Question: A patient with lactose intolerance lacks enough lactase, the enzyme that hydrolyzes lactose into
Distractors: glucose and glucose | glucose and fructose | galactose and fructose
Feedback: Lactose → galactose + glucose. Two glucose units come from maltose; glucose + fructose comes from sucrose.

Question: Which carbohydrate consists of exactly two glucose units joined by an α(1→4)-glycosidic bond?
Distractors: lactose | sucrose | amylose
Feedback: Starch digestion produces maltose, glucose–α(1→4)–glucose. Lactose is galactose–β(1→4)–glucose, sucrose contains fructose, and amylose is a long chain of many glucose units.

Question: In sucrose, glucose and fructose are joined by which glycosidic bond?
Feedback: C1 of α-glucose bonds to C2 of β-fructose: an α,β(1→2) linkage. Because both anomeric carbons are used, sucrose is not a reducing sugar.

Question: Humans can digest starch but not cellulose because cellulose contains
Distractors: fructose units in place of glucose units | α(1→6)-glycosidic bonds at branch points | galactose units in place of glucose units
Feedback: Cellulose is glucose joined by β(1→4) bonds, and human amylases hydrolyze only α bonds. Starch also has α(1→6) branches, so branching is not the difference; cellulose passes through as dietary fiber.

Question: Which statement best describes glycogen?
Correct answer: a highly branched glucose polymer stored in liver and muscle
Distractors: an unbranched glucose polymer stored in plants | a polymer of fructose stored in the liver | a structural polymer of β-glucose in plant cell walls
Feedback: Glycogen is α(1→4)-linked glucose with frequent α(1→6) branches, making it highly branched, stored in liver and muscle. Unbranched amylose is a plant starch; cellulose is the β structural polymer.

Question: Type B red blood cells carry an extra galactose unit on their surface markers that type O cells lack; type A cells carry an extra amino sugar (N-acetylgalactosamine) instead. The ABO blood types therefore differ in the
Correct answer: carbohydrate chains attached to the surface of red blood cells
Distractors: number of hemoglobin molecules inside each red blood cell | fatty acids in the phospholipids of the red cell membrane | amount of iron in the heme groups of the red blood cells
Feedback: All red cells carry a basic oligosaccharide (type O). Type A adds N-acetylgalactosamine, type B adds galactose, and type AB has both. So the blood types differ in the carbohydrate chains on the red blood cell surface, which is why mismatched transfusions trigger antibodies.

Question: Which pair of polysaccharides contains α(1→6)-glycosidic bonds at branch points?
Distractors: amylose and cellulose | amylose and amylopectin | cellulose and glycogen
Feedback: All three starch-type polymers have α(1→4) chains, but only amylopectin (branch about every 25 units) and glycogen (about every 10 units) also have α(1→6) branch points. Amylose is unbranched α(1→4); cellulose is unbranched β(1→4).

Question: An infant with galactosemia cannot convert galactose into glucose, so toxic galactose products build up. Which food must be removed from the infant's diet?
Distractors: table sugar, because sucrose contains galactose | bread, because starch contains galactose | fruit, because fructose contains galactose
Feedback: Lactose (milk sugar) is galactose + glucose, so milk and other lactose-containing foods must be removed. Sucrose is glucose + fructose, and starch contains only glucose.

Question: In lactose (milk sugar), carbon 1 of β-D-galactose is bonded through an oxygen atom to carbon 4 of D-glucose. How is this glycosidic linkage labeled?
Feedback: The anomeric carbon (C1) of galactose is in the β form and is joined to C4 of glucose, so the linkage is β(1→4). Lactase must break this β bond; α(1→4) is the linkage in maltose and starch.

Question: Amylose, amylopectin, glycogen and cellulose are all hydrolyzed completely to which monosaccharide?
Distractors: glucose and fructose | glucose and galactose | fructose only
Feedback: All four are polymers of glucose only; they differ in α versus β linkages and branching. Glucose + fructose make sucrose, and glucose + galactose make lactose.

Question: A dietitian notes that table sugar dissolves easily in water, but cooking oil does not. Which statement best explains why most simple carbohydrates are water soluble?
Correct answer: Their many –OH groups form hydrogen bonds with water
Distractors: Their glycosidic bonds ionize to form charged ions in water | Their long hydrocarbon chains attract water molecules | Their ester groups are hydrolyzed by water as they dissolve
Feedback: Sugars carry many polar –OH groups that hydrogen bond with water, so they dissolve. Lipids are mostly long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains with few H-bonding groups, so they are insoluble. Glycosidic bonds do not ionize.

Question: A food-science student heats four sugar solutions with Benedict's reagent (blue Cu2+). Which solution forms an orange-red precipitate?
Distractors: sucrose | sorbitol | gluconic acid
Feedback: Lactose keeps a free hemiacetal on its glucose unit, so it reduces Cu2+ to Cu2O. Sucrose has both anomeric carbons tied up; sorbitol has no carbonyl; gluconic acid is already oxidized.

Question: When D-galactose reacts with a mild oxidizing agent, its –CHO group is oxidized. What is the product?
Distractors: D-galactitol | D-gluconic acid | lactic acid
Feedback: The –CHO on C1 becomes –COOH, giving D-galactonic acid. D-galactitol (an '-itol' sugar alcohol) is the product of reduction, not oxidation.

Question: Salivary amylase begins hydrolyzing the amylose in a cracker while it is being chewed. Which disaccharide is a major product?
Distractors: lactose | sucrose | cellobiose
Feedback: Breaking amylose's α(1→4) chain into two-glucose pieces gives maltose (glucose–α(1→4)–glucose). Lactose and sucrose contain galactose or fructose; cellobiose has a β(1→4) bond, like cellulose.

Question: A biological polymer is hydrolyzed by dilute acid and gives only glucose. The bonds that held the monomers together are best described as which functional group?
Distractors: Ester linkages | Amide (peptide) linkages | Phosphodiester linkages
Feedback: A polymer of glucose is a polysaccharide (starch, glycogen or cellulose). Each glycosidic bond forms when the hemiacetal carbon of one glucose bonds through oxygen to an –OH of the next unit, giving an acetal (two –OR groups on one carbon). Esters link fatty acids in lipids, amides link amino acids in proteins and phosphodiesters link nucleotides.

Question: The liver attaches glucuronic acid to many drugs and to bilirubin (glucuronidation). Glucuronic acid is a uronic acid made from glucose. Which carbon(s) of glucose have been oxidized to –COOH in glucuronic acid?
Correct answer: only C6; C1 stays an aldehyde
Distractors: only C1; C6 stays –CH2OH | both C1 and C6 | only C2
Feedback: In a uronic (alduronic) acid, only the last carbon, C6, is oxidized to –COOH. C1 is untouched, so glucuronic acid is still a reducing sugar.

Question: Glucuronidation helps the kidneys excrete a drug in urine. Attaching glucuronic acid has this effect mainly because it
Correct answer: adds several polar –OH groups and an ionized –COO− group, making the drug more water soluble
Distractors: makes the drug more nonpolar so it dissolves in body fat | breaks the drug into CO2 and water | turns the drug into a polysaccharide that is stored in the liver
Feedback: Glucuronic acid has several –OH groups and a –COOH that is ionized (–COO−) at body pH. Attaching it makes the drug much more polar and water soluble, so the kidneys can excrete it in urine.

Question: The A1C test measures hemoglobin A1C, which forms when glucose attaches, without any enzyme, to an –NH2 group of hemoglobin. Which group of glucose reacts with the –NH2?
Correct answer: the aldehyde (C=O) group of the open-chain form
Distractors: the –OH on carbon 6 | a glycosidic bond | the oxygen atom inside the ring
Feedback: In its open-chain form, glucose has an aldehyde (C=O) at C1. This carbonyl reacts with an amino group on hemoglobin. The more glucose in the blood, the more hemoglobin becomes glycated.

Question: Why does an A1C result reflect a patient's average blood glucose over the past 2–3 months instead of only today's level?
Correct answer: Glucose stays attached to hemoglobin for the life of the red blood cell, about 120 days
Distractors: Hemoglobin is made only once every three months | Glucose needs three months to enter red blood cells | The A1C test measures glycogen stored in the liver
Feedback: Once glucose is attached to hemoglobin, it stays there for the rest of the red blood cell's life, about 120 days. So the percentage of glycated hemoglobin builds up in step with average blood glucose over the past few months.

Question: Lactose-free milk from Valley dairies is made by adding the enzyme lactase to milk. It tastes slightly sweeter than regular milk, even though no sugar is added. Why?
Correct answer: Lactase hydrolyzes lactose into glucose and galactose, which together taste sweeter than lactose
Distractors: Lactase converts lactose into sucrose | Lactase polymerizes lactose into starch | Removing lactose leaves only the milk proteins, which are sweet
Feedback: Lactase breaks the β(1→4) glycosidic bond, giving glucose and galactose. Together these monosaccharides taste sweeter than the same amount of lactose, and people who make little lactase can absorb them.

Question: Many people with lactose intolerance can eat yogurt or aged cheese with fewer symptoms than milk causes. What is the main reason?
Correct answer: Bacteria have already fermented much of the lactose into lactic acid
Distractors: The proteins in cheese block lactose from being digested | Cooking turns lactose into cellulose | Yogurt contains more lactose than milk, which trains the body to make lactase
Feedback: During fermentation, bacteria break down much of the milk's lactose and turn it into lactic acid (which makes yogurt tangy). In cheese, more lactose also leaves with the whey. Less lactose remains, so less reaches the colon undigested.

Question: Fructose is a ketose, with no aldehyde group, yet it gives a positive Benedict's test. Why?
Correct answer: In the basic test solution fructose rearranges into an aldose, and the aldose is oxidized
Distractors: The ketone group of fructose is oxidized directly to a carboxylic acid | Benedict's reagent first hydrolyzes fructose into two smaller aldehydes | Fructose is a nonreducing sugar, and nonreducing sugars turn the reagent red
Feedback: Benedict's reagent is basic, and in base a ketose is in equilibrium with an aldose. The aldose form has an aldehyde that is oxidized, so fructose reduces Cu2+ and counts as a reducing sugar.

Question: A glucose solution is heated with blue Benedict's reagent and a brick-red solid forms. Which statement describes the redox change?
Correct answer: Glucose is oxidized and Cu2+ is reduced to Cu2O
Distractors: Glucose is reduced and Cu2+ is oxidized to Cu2O | Glucose is oxidized and Cu+ is oxidized to Cu2+ | Glucose is reduced to sorbitol and the copper is unchanged
Feedback: The aldehyde of glucose is oxidized to a carboxylic acid (gluconic acid). The electrons go to copper: blue Cu2+ is reduced to copper(I) in brick-red Cu2O. Glucose is the reducing agent.

Question: A student heats four solutions with Benedict's reagent: glucose, fructose, maltose and xylitol (the sweetener in sugar-free gum). Which solution stays blue?
Distractors: glucose | fructose | maltose
Feedback: Xylitol is a sugar alcohol: the C=O of xylose has been reduced to one more –OH carbon. With no carbonyl and no hemiacetal there is nothing to oxidize, so the test is negative and the solution stays blue.

Question: Mannitol is made from the aldohexose mannose by reaction with H2 and a metal catalyst. What change takes place?
Correct answer: The –CHO group at C1 is reduced to –CH2OH, giving a sugar alcohol
Distractors: The –CHO group at C1 is oxidized to –COOH, giving an aldonic acid | The –CH2OH group at C6 is oxidized to –COOH, giving a uronic acid | Both ends of the chain are oxidized to –COOH, giving an aldaric acid
Feedback: H2 with a metal catalyst is a reduction. It turns the aldehyde C=O into an alcohol, so mannose becomes mannitol, a sugar alcohol (alditol) with an –OH on every carbon.

Question: Glucose is warmed with Tollens' reagent, which contains Ag+. What is seen, and what does the glucose become?
Correct answer: A silver mirror forms; glucose becomes gluconic acid
Distractors: A silver mirror forms; glucose becomes sorbitol | A brick-red solid forms; glucose becomes glucaric acid | Nothing happens, because only ketoses react with Tollens' reagent
Feedback: Tollens' reagent oxidizes only the aldehyde at C1, so glucose becomes gluconic acid (an aldonic acid). The Ag+ is reduced to silver metal, which coats the glass as a silver mirror.

Question: A drop of iodine solution turns deep blue-violet on a slice of potato. Which polysaccharide causes this color, and why?
Correct answer: Amylose, because its coiled chain traps iodine inside the helix
Distractors: Cellulose, because its straight chains pack around iodine | Glycogen, because its many branches trap iodine | Amylopectin, because iodine breaks its α(1→6) branch points
Feedback: Amylose is an unbranched α(1→4) chain that coils into a helix with six glucose units per turn. Iodine fits inside the amylose helix, and that complex is deep blue-violet.

Question: Glycogen has α(1→6) branch points about every 8–12 glucose units, more often than amylopectin. How does the extra branching help an animal?
Correct answer: A branched molecule has many chain ends, so enzymes can release glucose from many places at once
Distractors: The branch points are β links, which makes glycogen resistant to digestion | Branching lets glycogen store fructose and galactose as well as glucose | Branching lets the chains line up side by side into strong fibers
Feedback: Glycogen phosphorylase removes glucose units from chain ends. More branches mean more ends, so glucose can be released quickly between meals or during exercise.

Question: Cotton is about 95% cellulose. It is strong and does not dissolve in water, even though every glucose unit has several –OH groups. What explains this?
Correct answer: The straight β(1→4) chains lie side by side and hydrogen bond to each other, forming tightly packed fibers
Distractors: Cellulose is highly branched, and the branches tangle together | The –OH groups of glucose are lost when the glycosidic bonds form, so cellulose is nonpolar | The chains coil into helices that hide the –OH groups from water
Feedback: The β(1→4) links make cellulose an extended, linear chain. Neighboring chains hydrogen bond to each other and pack into fibers, so the –OH groups are used up holding the chains together instead of interacting with water.

Question: Which statement about plant starch is correct?
Correct answer: It is a mixture of amylose (unbranched) and amylopectin (branched), with more amylopectin
Distractors: It is a mixture of amylose (branched) and amylopectin (unbranched), with more amylose | It is a mixture of amylose and cellulose | It is a single branched polymer that is identical to glycogen
Feedback: Starch is about 20% amylose, a linear α(1→4) chain, and about 80% amylopectin, which has α(1→6) branch points. Both give only glucose on complete hydrolysis.

Question: A cow gets glucose from the cellulose in grass, but a person cannot. What is the reason?
Correct answer: Microorganisms in the cow's digestive tract make cellulase, which hydrolyzes β(1→4) links
Distractors: The cow's own amylase hydrolyzes β(1→4) links more slowly than α(1→4) links | Cellulose in grass is made of a different monosaccharide than cellulose in human food | Stomach acid in a cow is strong enough to change the β links into α links
Feedback: Animals do not make an enzyme for the β(1→4) links of cellulose. Microorganisms living in the cow's gut make cellulase, which hydrolyzes cellulose to glucose; humans have no such help, so cellulose passes through as fiber.

Question: These fatty acids all have 18 carbons. Which has the lowest melting point?
Distractors: linoleic acid (2 cis double bonds) | oleic acid (1 cis double bond) | stearic acid (no double bonds)
Feedback: More cis kinks mean poorer packing and weaker dispersion forces, so linolenic acid melts lowest (about −11 °C). Saturated stearic acid packs best and melts highest; this is why oils are liquid and butter is solid.

Question: Linolenic acid is an omega-3 fatty acid. “Omega-3” means that
Correct answer: the first double bond is 3 carbons from the methyl (CH3) end
Distractors: it has three double bonds | the first double bond is at carbon 3 from the –COOH end | it has 3 carbons fewer than stearic acid
Feedback: Omega numbering counts from the CH3 (omega) end: the first C=C starts at carbon 3 from that end. Linolenic acid happens to have three double bonds too, but that is not what ω-3 means.

Question: A triacylglycerol (triglyceride) is formed from
Correct answer: glycerol and three fatty acids joined by ester bonds
Distractors: glycerol and three fatty acids joined by amide bonds | cholesterol and three fatty acids | sphingosine, a fatty acid and phosphate
Feedback: Each –OH of glycerol forms an ester with a fatty acid: glycerol + 3 fatty acids. Sphingosine is the backbone of sphingolipids.

Question: How many moles of NaOH are needed to completely saponify 1 mole of a triacylglycerol?
Feedback: A triacylglycerol has three ester bonds, so 3 mol NaOH give glycerol and three moles of sodium fatty-acid salts (soap).

Question: A triacylglycerol contains one oleic acid (1 C=C) and two linoleic acids (2 C=C each). How many moles of H2 are needed to fully hydrogenate 1 mole of it?
Feedback: 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 mol H2. Answering 3 counts the fatty acids instead of the double bonds. The ester C=O groups are not hydrogenated.

Question: Beeswax and carnauba wax (used in dental impression materials and car polish) are
Correct answer: esters of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol
Distractors: triacylglycerols made only from saturated fatty acids | steroids built from four fused carbon rings | phospholipids with a choline head group
Feedback: A wax is one ester made from a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol, which makes it very water-repellent. Triacylglycerols contain glycerol.

Question: Lecithin, a glycerophospholipid, contains glycerol, two fatty acids, a phosphate group and
Distractors: a third fatty acid chain | sphingosine, a long-chain base | cholesterol, a steroid
Feedback: Lecithin = phosphatidylcholine: glycerol + 2 fatty acids + phosphate + choline. A third fatty acid would make a triacylglycerol.

Question: Sphingomyelin, abundant in the myelin sheath around nerve cells, differs from glycerophospholipids because its backbone is
Distractors: glycerol, a three-carbon triol | cholesterol, a steroid alcohol | a long-chain fatty acid
Feedback: Sphingolipids are built on sphingosine; its amino group forms an amide with one fatty acid. Glycerophospholipids are built on glycerol.

Question: Cholesterol, the sex hormones and cortisone are steroids. All steroids contain
Distractors: three fatty acids bonded to a glycerol backbone | a long-chain fatty acid joined by an ester bond | a phosphate head group and two fatty-acid tails
Feedback: The steroid nucleus is four fused rings: three cyclohexane rings and one cyclopentane ring. Cholesterol adds an –OH and a hydrocarbon side chain.

Question: Aspirin and ibuprofen reduce pain and inflammation by blocking the COX enzyme, which converts arachidonic acid (a 20-carbon fatty acid) into a family of eicosanoids. Which lipids do these drugs keep the body from making?
Correct answer: prostaglandins, which contain a five-membered ring
Distractors: steroids, which contain four fused rings | triacylglycerols, which contain three ester bonds | sphingolipids, which contain a sphingosine backbone
Feedback: COX converts arachidonic acid into prostaglandins, the eicosanoids that cause pain, fever and inflammation; blocking COX is how NSAIDs work. Steroids are made from cholesterol, and triacylglycerols and sphingolipids are not eicosanoids.

Question: Partial hydrogenation of vegetable oils is a health concern mainly because it
Correct answer: converts some cis double bonds to trans
Distractors: adds cholesterol to the vegetable oil | breaks the ester bonds to glycerol | makes the fatty acids more unsaturated
Feedback: Some remaining double bonds isomerize to the trans form; trans fats raise LDL cholesterol and the risk of heart disease. Hydrogenation makes fats less, not more, unsaturated, and plant oils contain no cholesterol.

Question: LDL carries cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues, where excess can deposit in artery walls. HDL is often called “good cholesterol” because it
Correct answer: carries cholesterol from the tissues back to the liver
Distractors: carries cholesterol from the liver out to the tissues | carries more triacylglycerol than any other lipoprotein | carries only phospholipid and protein, with no cholesterol
Feedback: HDL picks up excess cholesterol from tissues and returns it to the liver, where it can be made into bile salts and removed. LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues, and high LDL leads to plaque (atherosclerosis). Chylomicrons carry the most triacylglycerol.

Question: Linoleic acid and linolenic acid are called essential fatty acids because
Correct answer: the body cannot make them, so they must come from the diet
Distractors: they are the only fatty acids found in cell membranes | they are saturated and provide the most energy per gram | the body makes them from glucose when the diet lacks fat
Feedback: Humans cannot put double bonds at the omega-3 and omega-6 positions, so these polyunsaturated fatty acids must be obtained from food. They are unsaturated, not saturated.

Question: Butter and lard are solids at room temperature, while olive oil is a liquid. The best explanation is that the animal fats contain more
Correct answer: saturated fatty acids, whose straight chains pack closely
Distractors: unsaturated fatty acids, whose cis kinks pack closely | glycerol per molecule, which raises the melting point | short-chain fatty acids, which form hydrogen bonds
Feedback: Saturated chains are straight and pack closely, giving stronger dispersion forces and higher melting points. Cis double bonds put kinks in the chains, so oils (mostly unsaturated) pack poorly and stay liquid. Every triacylglycerol has exactly one glycerol.

Question: Which lipid does NOT undergo saponification with NaOH?
Distractors: beeswax | lecithin | glyceryl tripalmitate
Feedback: Waxes, glycerophospholipids such as lecithin, and triacylglycerols all contain ester bonds that NaOH hydrolyzes. Cholesterol is a steroid alcohol with no ester group, so it is nonsaponifiable.

Question: Which biomolecule contains ester linkages as its key functional group?
Distractors: amylose (a starch) | a tripeptide | cholesterol
Feedback: A triacylglycerol is glycerol esterified with three fatty acids (three ester bonds). Amylose has acetal (glycosidic) links, a tripeptide has amide (peptide) bonds, and cholesterol is a steroid alcohol with no ester.

Question: An 18-carbon fatty acid has one double bond, between C9 and C10 (counting the carboxyl carbon as C1). How is it classified?
Distractors: an omega-10 fatty acid | an omega-3 fatty acid | an omega-6 fatty acid
Feedback: The ω carbon is C18 (ω1), so C10 is 18 − 10 + 1 = ω9. The double bond starts 9 carbons from the methyl end: omega-9 (this is oleic acid in olive oil). Omega-10 comes from counting to C9 instead.

Question: Which structural description fits a prostaglandin, an eicosanoid that causes inflammation?
Correct answer: a 20-carbon fatty acid with a five-membered carbon ring
Distractors: four fused carbon rings with an –OH group on the first ring | glycerol joined to three long fatty acid chains by ester bonds | sphingosine bonded to a fatty acid, phosphate and choline
Feedback: Prostaglandins are made from arachidonic acid (20 C) and contain a five-membered ring within the 20-carbon fatty acid chain. Four fused rings describes a steroid; glycerol + 3 fatty acids is a triacylglycerol; the last choice is sphingomyelin.

Question: A triacylglycerol is heated with water and a strong acid catalyst (acid hydrolysis). What are the products?
Distractors: glycerol and three fatty acid salts (soap) | three glycerol molecules and one fatty acid | one fatty acid and a diacylglycerol ester
Feedback: Acid hydrolysis breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three free fatty acids. Base hydrolysis (saponification with NaOH) gives glycerol and three fatty acid salts, which are soaps.

Question: Palmitoleic acid, found in macadamia nut oil, is CH3(CH2)5CH=CH(CH2)7COOH. Counting from the methyl (omega) end, which type of fatty acid is it?
Distractors: omega-9 | omega-6 | omega-3
Feedback: CH3 is ω1, the five CH2 groups are ω2–ω6, so the double bond starts at ω7: an omega-7 fatty acid. Counting from the –COOH end puts the double bond at C9, which is the tempting omega-9 mistake.

Question: Rank by chain length: lauric, myristic, palmitic and stearic acids are saturated and occur in animal fats. Which one stays solid to the highest temperature?
Distractors: palmitic acid (16 C) | myristic acid (14 C) | lauric acid (12 C)
Feedback: Longer saturated chains have more surface contact and stronger dispersion forces, so they melt at higher temperatures. The 18-carbon stearic acid melts highest.

Question: A soap maker heats glyceryl tripalmitate (a triacylglycerol made from three palmitic acids) with aqueous KOH. What are the products?
Distractors: glycerol and three palmitic acid | three glycerol and one potassium palmitate | glycerol and one potassium palmitate
Feedback: Base breaks all three ester bonds, giving glycerol and three potassium palmitate (soap). Free palmitic acid forms only in acid hydrolysis; in KOH the acid is deprotonated to its K+ salt.

Question: A soap maker converts 0.250 mol of olive-oil triacylglycerol into soap. What mass of sodium hydroxide (40.00 g mol⁻¹) does the reaction consume?
Feedback: Each triacylglycerol needs 3 NaOH: 0.250 mol × 3 = 0.750 mol NaOH × 40.00 g mol⁻¹ = 30.0 g. Using a 1 : 1 ratio gives 10.0 g.

Question: A lipid from brain tissue is hydrolyzed. The products are sphingosine, one fatty acid and galactose; no phosphate or glycerol is found. What type of lipid is it?
Distractors: a sphingomyelin | a glycerophospholipid | a wax
Feedback: A sphingosine backbone with a monosaccharide head group and no phosphate is a glycolipid (cerebroside). Sphingomyelin also has sphingosine but carries a phosphate–choline head group.

Question: A nutrition label separates fats into saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated. Which of these fatty acids belongs in the polyunsaturated group?
Correct answer: linoleic acid, with two C=C bonds
Distractors: oleic acid, with one C=C bond | stearic acid, with no C=C bonds | palmitic acid, with no C=C bonds
Feedback: A polyunsaturated fatty acid has two or more C=C bonds, so linoleic acid fits. Oleic acid, with one C=C, is monounsaturated; stearic and palmitic acids are saturated.

Question: When glycerol reacts with three fatty acids to make one triacylglycerol, how many ester bonds form and how many water molecules are released?
Distractors: 3 ester bonds; 1 H2O | 1 ester bond; 3 H2O | 3 ester bonds; 6 H2O
Feedback: Each of glycerol's three –OH groups condenses with one –COOH, forming one ester bond and losing one water each time: 3 ester bonds and 3 H2O.

Question: Two students break down samples of the same vegetable oil (a triacylglycerol): one uses hot water with an H2SO4 catalyst, the other uses aqueous NaOH. Compare the products of the two experiments.
Correct answer: Glycerol forms in each case; acid gives free fatty acids, NaOH gives fatty acid salts (soaps)
Distractors: Acid gives glycerol and fatty acids; NaOH gives glycerol and three alcohols | Acid gives three esters; NaOH gives glycerol and fatty acids | Fatty acid salts form in each case; only NaOH releases glycerol
Feedback: Either way the three ester bonds are hydrolyzed and the alcohol portion, glycerol, is released. In acid the carboxylic acids are freed as RCOOH; in NaOH the base neutralizes them to RCOO−Na+, the salts we call soap. Fatty acids are the acid part of the ester, so they are never released as alcohols.

Question: Phospholipids form the bilayer of cell membranes, but triacylglycerols do not; they collect as droplets inside fat cells. Why?
Correct answer: A triacylglycerol has no polar, charged head group, so it is nonpolar throughout
Distractors: A triacylglycerol has only one fatty acid tail | Triacylglycerols are too water soluble to stay in a membrane | Triacylglycerols contain a steroid ring that is too rigid
Feedback: In a phospholipid one ester is replaced by a charged phosphate–amino alcohol head, so the molecule is amphipathic and lines up with heads toward water. In a triacylglycerol all three glycerol –OH groups are esterified to fatty acids, leaving no polar head; the whole molecule is nonpolar, so it simply clumps into oily droplets.

Question: A food company hydrogenates 2.0 mol of a cooking oil whose triacylglycerol contains one palmitic acid (16:0), one oleic acid (18:1) and one linoleic acid (18:2). What amount of H2 is consumed, and how does the melting point change?
Distractors: 3.0 mol H2; melting point rises | 6.0 mol H2; melting point falls | 2.0 mol H2; melting point is unchanged
Feedback: One molecule has 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 C=C bonds, so 1 mol of fat needs 3 mol H2 and 2.0 mol needs 6.0 mol H2. Removing the cis kinks lets the chains pack tightly, so the melting point rises (an oil becomes a solid fat). "3.0 mol" forgets the 2.0 mol of fat.

Question: Prostaglandins, thromboxanes and leukotrienes are all made from the same starting material. What is it?
Correct answer: arachidonic acid, a 20-carbon polyunsaturated fatty acid released from membrane phospholipids
Distractors: cholesterol, a steroid | glycerol | sphingosine, an amino alcohol
Feedback: All eicosanoids come from arachidonic acid, a 20-carbon fatty acid with four cis C=C bonds that is cut out of membrane phospholipids when needed.

Question: Flaxseed oil turns rancid by reacting with O2 in the air much faster than coconut oil does. What is the best explanation?
Correct answer: Flaxseed oil has many C=C double bonds, which O2 attacks; coconut oil is mostly saturated
Distractors: Flaxseed oil has more ester bonds per molecule than coconut oil | Saturated fats react with O2 faster than unsaturated fats | Coconut oil contains no carbon–hydrogen bonds
Feedback: Oxygen attacks fatty acid chains at and next to their C=C bonds. Flaxseed oil is rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids with many C=C bonds, while coconut oil is mostly saturated, so flaxseed oil oxidizes and turns rancid faster.

Question: Butter left out too long smells sour and "cheesy" because butyric acid (a 4-carbon fatty acid) is released. Which reaction releases it?
Correct answer: hydrolysis of the ester bonds of the triacylglycerols, catalyzed by lipases from microbes
Distractors: hydrogenation of the C=C bonds | saponification with NaOH | dehydration of glycerol
Feedback: This is hydrolytic rancidity: lipase enzymes from microorganisms hydrolyze the ester bonds of butterfat, releasing free short-chain fatty acids such as butyric acid, which are volatile and smell bad.

Question: Valley citrus packing houses coat lemons and oranges with a thin layer of food-grade wax (such as carnauba wax) to reduce water loss. Why is a wax good at keeping water in?
Correct answer: A wax is an ester with long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains on both sides, so it repels water
Distractors: A wax is very polar and hydrogen bonds strongly to water | A wax is a triacylglycerol with three polar ester groups | A wax is a steroid with an –OH group that traps water
Feedback: A wax is an ester of a long-chain fatty acid and a long-chain alcohol. Except for one small ester group, it is all long nonpolar hydrocarbon chains, so it repels water and forms a waterproof barrier, like the natural wax on fruit peel.

Question: A handful of Valley almonds supplies a good share of the day's vitamin E (α-tocopherol), an antioxidant that protects the polyunsaturated fatty acid chains in cell membranes. Which part of vitamin E gives up an H atom to stop the oxidation?
Correct answer: the phenol –OH group on its ring
Distractors: its long hydrocarbon tail | an ester group | a carboxylic acid group
Feedback: Vitamin E gives up the H of its phenol –OH to a reactive oxygen species, stopping the chain of oxidation before it spreads through the membrane's fatty acid chains.

Question: Fluconazole, a drug used to treat Valley fever (coccidioidomycosis), blocks a fungal enzyme needed to make ergosterol, the four-ring lipid that fungal cell membranes use in place of cholesterol. To which lipid class does ergosterol belong?
Distractors: triacylglycerol | glycerophospholipid | wax
Feedback: Four fused carbon rings (three six-membered and one five-membered) define a steroid. Ergosterol is the fungal steroid that does the job cholesterol does in human membranes, so blocking its synthesis damages the fungal membrane.

Question: In the fluid-mosaic model of a cell membrane, the phospholipid bilayer is arranged with
Correct answer: polar heads facing the water and nonpolar tails inside
Distractors: nonpolar tails facing the water and polar heads inside | all molecules lying flat on the cell surface | proteins forming the inner layer
Feedback: The hydrophilic heads face the watery inside and outside of the cell while the hydrophobic fatty-acid tails point toward each other in the middle. Proteins float in this layer, like a mosaic.

Question: Glucose moves into red blood cells from higher to lower concentration through a specific membrane protein, without using ATP. This is
Distractors: active transport | simple diffusion | secondary active transport
Feedback: Movement down a concentration gradient with no energy input is passive; because it needs a protein carrier it is facilitated transport. Simple diffusion needs no protein (small nonpolar molecules such as O2), and active transport uses ATP to move against a gradient.

Question: During β-oxidation, a fatty acyl chain is oxidized at its β carbon. Counting the carboxyl carbon as C1, which carbon is the β carbon?
Correct answer: C3, two carbons away from the carboxyl carbon
Distractors: C2, the carbon right next to the carboxyl carbon | C1, the carboxyl (acyl) carbon itself | the CH3 carbon at the far end of the chain
Feedback: The α carbon is C2 (attached to the carboxyl carbon) and the β carbon is C3. The CH3 carbon at the far end is the ω (omega) carbon, used to name omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.

Question: Testosterone, estradiol, cortisol and aldosterone are hormones made in the body from which lipid?
Distractors: arachidonic acid | sphingosine | lecithin
Feedback: These are steroid hormones; their four fused rings come from cholesterol. Arachidonic acid is the starting material for eicosanoids (prostaglandins), not steroids.

Question: Which substance crosses a cell membrane mainly by simple diffusion through the lipid bilayer?
Distractors: glucose | Na+ | K+
Feedback: Small, nonpolar or uncharged molecules such as O2, CO2 and (to some extent) H2O diffuse directly through the bilayer. Glucose needs a carrier protein (facilitated transport), and charged ions need channels or pumps.

Question: Nerve cells use the Na+/K+ pump, which uses ATP to move 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, both from lower to higher concentration. This is an example of
Distractors: simple diffusion | facilitated transport | osmosis
Feedback: Moving ions against their concentration gradients requires energy from ATP: active transport. Facilitated transport also uses a protein, but moves solutes from higher to lower concentration with no ATP.

Question: Elaidic acid is the trans isomer of oleic acid (an 18-carbon acid with one cis double bond). Elaidic acid melts at a much higher temperature than oleic acid. Why?
Correct answer: The trans chains are nearly straight and pack closely.
Distractors: The trans double bond adds hydrogen bonds between chains. | Elaidic acid has fewer carbon atoms than oleic acid has. | The trans double bond puts a sharper kink in each chain.
Feedback: A cis double bond puts a kink in the chain that keeps chains apart. A trans double bond leaves the chain nearly straight, so the chains pack closely, raising the melting point, which is why trans fats behave like saturated fats.

Question: Which lipoprotein carries cholesterol from the liver to the body's tissues, and is linked to plaque buildup in arteries when its level is high?
Distractors: HDL | chylomicron | VLDL
Feedback: LDL (low-density lipoprotein) delivers cholesterol to cells; when it is high, cholesterol deposits in artery walls. HDL does the opposite, returning cholesterol to the liver.

Question: Triolein, a liquid oil, contains three oleic acids (18 carbons, one cis C=C each). It is completely hydrogenated with H2 and a Ni catalyst. What is the product?
Distractors: tripalmitin, a liquid oil | glycerol and three oleic acids | trilinolein, a liquid oil
Feedback: Adding H2 to each C=C turns every 18-carbon oleic acid into stearic acid, so the product is tristearin, a solid fat. Hydrogenation does not break the ester bonds (that would be hydrolysis) or shorten the chains.

Question: Cholesterol makes up about 25% of the lipid in some animal cell membranes. What is its main role there?
Correct answer: It fits between phospholipid tails and regulates membrane fluidity.
Distractors: It forms channels that carry ions across the membrane. | It provides the polar head groups that face the water. | It is broken down in the membrane to supply energy.
Feedback: Rigid cholesterol molecules slip between the fatty acid tails, keeping the membrane from becoming too fluid or too rigid. Ion channels are membrane proteins, and cholesterol is not used as a fuel.

Question: Lipids are grouped together as a class not by a shared functional group but by a shared property. Which property defines a lipid?
Correct answer: Insoluble in water but soluble in nonpolar solvents
Distractors: Soluble in water because of many –OH groups | Made of repeating amino acid units | Always contains a phosphate group
Feedback: A lipid is defined as a biomolecule that is insoluble in water and soluble in nonpolar solvents such as hexane or ether, because most of its structure is hydrocarbon. Carbohydrates are the water-soluble polyhydroxy compounds; only phospholipids contain phosphate, and proteins are the amino acid polymers.

Question: Cholesterol is the starting material for several hormones. Which hormone is NOT made from cholesterol?
Distractors: Testosterone | Cortisol | Estradiol
